problem: Shelter-based approaches were not ending long-term homelessness.
title: Finland adopts Housing First, giving homeless people permanent homes without preconditions
actor_name: Government of Finland and the Y-Foundation
context: Finland had long-term homelessness and relied heavily on shelters.
decision_made: Provide permanent housing first, with support services, instead of requiring people to become housing-ready.
action_taken: Converted shelters into housing; the number of shelter and hostel beds in Helsinki reportedly fell from 2,121 in 1985 to 52 in 2016.
observed_outcome: The European Commission reports homelessness fell for 11 consecutive years by 2023, with a 40 percent fall from 2008 to 2019, and the Y-Foundation reports long-term homelessness decreasing for over a decade.
lessons: Housing first can reduce homelessness when paired with supply of homes and support, though it is limited in scope.
limitations: Much of the evidence is from the Y-Foundation, which is an advocate. A headline claim of a 75 percent reduction was not verified. Sources mix different periods.

claims.claim_text: Finland introduced a Housing First approach to homelessness in 2008.
The European Commission reports overall homelessness declined for 11 consecutive years by 2023.
